question: Mickey Mouse, Bugs Bunny and many other classic cartoon characters wear white gloves, even though they are animals. What practical problem did those gloves solve for early animators?
correct_answer: Hands stayed visible against black bodies
alternative_answers: Black hands disappeared against black bodies
To make the hands easier to see
To make hand movements readable on screen
Hands were simpler and faster to draw
To make the characters look more human
headline_answer: Hands stayed visible against black bodies
source_excerpt: black hands couldn't be seen against black bodies in black-and-white films, so white gloves solved this issue.

extra.verification_notes: The widely cited reason is that black hands were invisible against black bodies in black-and-white animation; other reasons (easier drawing, vaudeville tradition) exist but visibility is the standard practical answer (https://collider.com/cartoon-characters-gloves/).

explanation: Early cartoons were drawn in black and white, and characters like Mickey Mouse had solid black bodies with equally black hands. Whenever a hand passed in front of the body it simply disappeared, so gestures were unreadable. Bright white gloves gave the hands contrast and let audiences follow every movement. The gloves also made hands rounder and simpler, which was faster to draw thousands of times, and they made the animal characters feel more human. Walt Disney later said Mickey got gloves so he would not have mouse hands, because he was meant to seem more like a person.

question: In his very first comics in 1938, Superman could not fly. How did he get over tall buildings instead?
source_excerpt: In Action Comics #1, Superman possesses superhuman speed, allowing him to run and leap... but lacks flight.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume flight is Superman's most basic power; the original Superman was a jumper, which the famous 'single bound' line still preserves.
extra.verification_notes: Superman in Action Comics #1 (1938) could not fly and instead leaped over buildings; later flight was added, per Wikipedia.

explanation: The early Superman simply leaped enormous distances, which is why the old slogan says he could leap tall buildings in a single bound. True flight was only added a few years later.

question: The letters 'DC' in the publisher name DC Comics are an abbreviation of which of the company's own comic-book titles?
source_excerpt: DC is an initialism for Detective Comics, a comic book series first published in 1937.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone says 'DC Comics' without noticing the name literally means 'Detective Comics Comics'; the answer feels obvious once heard, especially since Batman fans know Detective Comics #27.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms DC is an initialism for Detective Comics; no name change found (only a 2024 logo refresh).

explanation: Detective Comics was the anthology in which Batman first appeared in 1939, and the title became so identified with the company that its initials became the brand.

question: Wonder Woman's creator, William Moulton Marston, was a psychologist who helped develop which machine, a fitting origin for a heroine with a Lasso of Truth?
source_excerpt: systolic blood pressure test, which became one component of the modern polygraph

extra.why_interesting: Wonder Woman's Lasso of Truth suddenly makes sense: her creator spent his scientific career trying to detect lies.
extra.verification_notes: Marston created the systolic blood pressure test that became a component of the modern polygraph (lie detector), so 'helped develop' is accurate; Larson built the device itself.

explanation: Marston devised the blood-pressure test that became a core part of the polygraph, so a magic lasso that forces people to tell the truth was very much on brand.

question: In his 1962 debut issue, the Incredible Hulk was not green. What colour was he?
source_excerpt: After seeing the first published issue, Lee chose to change the skin color to green.

extra.why_interesting: The Hulk is practically defined by being green, so a debut in another colour is a genuine jolt; grey is guessable as a 'monster' colour.
extra.verification_notes: Hulk was grey in Incredible Hulk #1 (1962); Lee changed to green afterward due to colouring inconsistencies.

explanation: Stan Lee wanted a grey monster, but the printers could not keep the shade consistent from page to page, so from the second issue the Hulk turned green and stayed that way.

question: Walt Disney's honorary Oscar for Snow White came with one full-size statuette plus how many miniature ones?
source_excerpt: a special Academy Award consisting of one full-size and seven miniature Oscar statuettes

extra.why_interesting: The player may not know the trophy, but the title of the film hands them the number; the delight is realising the Academy actually did the obvious joke.
extra.verification_notes: Search results from the Walt Disney Family Museum describe the 1938 honorary award as one full-size plus seven miniature Oscar statuettes, matching the claimed answer.

explanation: One tall Oscar for Snow White and seven little ones for the dwarfs, handed over by child star Shirley Temple at the 1939 ceremony.

question: True or false: Simpsons creator Matt Groening named Homer Simpson after his own father.
source_excerpt: Groening named Homer after his father, who himself had been named after the ancient Greek poet.

extra.why_interesting: Homer sounds like a deliberate classical joke, so players suspect a trap; the truth is more personal and more charming.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Groening named Homer after his father, Homer Groening.

explanation: Groening's father really was called Homer, and his mother Margaret and sisters Lisa and Maggie lent their names too. Only Bart was invented.

question: In 1965 France became the third country to launch its own satellite. The satellite was named after which comic-book character?
source_excerpt: France also became the third country after the USSR and US to launch a satellite on its own rocket

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a satellite to carry a stately name; France chose a small, stubborn cartoon Gaul, and the clue 'France' plus 'comic character' leads a thoughtful player straight there.
extra.verification_notes: Astérix was launched 26 Nov 1965 and named after the comic character; France was third country to launch on its own rocket (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astérix_(satellite)).

explanation: The small Gaulish warrior who resists the Roman Empire was a national hero by 1965, and the satellite Astérix is still in orbit today.

question: Tintin walked on the Moon in Hergé's album published in 1954. How many years later did Neil Armstrong do it for real?
source_excerpt: Explorers on the Moon is the seventeenth volume of The Adventures of Tintin, published by Casterman in 1954, created by Hergé.

extra.why_interesting: Players know 1969 but rarely realise how early Tintin got there; working out the gap turns a trivia fact into a small 'aha'.
extra.verification_notes: Explorers on the Moon was published by Casterman as an album in 1954 and Armstrong walked on the Moon in 1969, a gap of 15 years (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explorers_on_the_Moon).

explanation: Apollo 11 landed in July 1969, fifteen years after the album Explorers on the Moon, which even got details like weightlessness and a multi-stage rocket broadly right.

question: On the 1969 Apollo 10 mission, the command module was nicknamed Charlie Brown. Which comic-strip character lent his name to the lunar module?
source_excerpt: The command module was given the call sign Charlie Brown and the lunar module the call sign Snoopy. These were taken from the characters in the comic strip, Peanuts.

extra.why_interesting: A NASA mission flying under cartoon names is surprising, but the Charlie Brown clue gives every player a fair path to the beagle.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Apollo 10's CM was Charlie Brown and its LM was Snoopy, both from Peanuts; this is a settled historical fact.

explanation: The lunar module Snoopy flew down to within about 15 kilometres of the Moon's surface as a dress rehearsal for Apollo 11, and Snoopy remains NASA's safety mascot to this day.

question: Eiichiro Oda's pirate manga One Piece holds the world record for copies of a single comic series by one author. Roughly how many copies are in circulation?
source_excerpt: over 600 million copies in circulation worldwide

extra.why_interesting: Western players underestimate manga; the true figure puts a single comic series in the same league as the best-selling novels in history.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports over 600 million copies in circulation by March 2026, and says the series holds the Guinness record for most copies of a comic series by a single author (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Piece).

explanation: More than 500 million copies of One Piece have been printed since 1997, which rivals the entire Harry Potter book series.

question: Wolverine did not debut in an X-Men comic. In 1974 he was introduced as a Canadian government agent sent to fight which Marvel giant?
source_excerpt: In his first mission, he is dispatched to stop the destruction caused by a brawl between the Hulk and the Wendigo.

extra.why_interesting: Wolverine is the X-Men's defining character, so fans are surprised he started as a guest villain in someone else's book; the Canadian clue plus 'another hero' narrows it fairly.
extra.verification_notes: Wolverine debuted in Incredible Hulk #180-181 (1974) as a Canadian agent sent against the Hulk; the Wendigo was also in the fight, which is a minor ambiguity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverine_(character)).

explanation: Wolverine appeared on the final page of The Incredible Hulk issue 180 and fought both the Hulk and the monster Wendigo in issue 181, a year before he joined the X-Men.

question: The cartoon dog Scooby-Doo was named after a scat phrase Frank Sinatra sings at the end of which of his 1966 hit songs?
alternative_answers: Strangers in the Night by Sinatra
source_excerpt: Silverman came up with the name from the scat syllables in Frank Sinatra's song 'Strangers in the Night'

extra.why_interesting: Nobody expects a Saturday-morning cartoon dog to be named after a Sinatra ad-lib; players who know the song's scat ending get a satisfying click.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Fred Silverman derived the name Scooby-Doo from Sinatra's scat 'doo-be-doo-be-doo' in 'Strangers in the Night' (1966).

explanation: Sinatra fades out singing 'doo-be-doo-be-doo', and television executive Fred Silverman heard it on a flight and turned it into the name of the Great Dane.

question: Tintin, the Smurfs and the cowboy Lucky Luke were all created by cartoonists from which European country?
source_excerpt: Western comic album series created by Belgian cartoonist, Maurice De Bevere, best known by the pen name Morris, in 1946.

extra.why_interesting: Players tend to file Tintin as French, the Smurfs as American because of the cartoon, and Lucky Luke as a Wild West import, when in fact one small country produced all three.
extra.verification_notes: Hergé (Tintin), Peyo (Smurfs) and Morris (Lucky Luke) were all Belgian; see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucky_Luke

explanation: Hergé, Peyo and Morris were all Belgian, and Brussels still celebrates its comic-strip heritage with murals and a dedicated museum.

question: Wonder Woman was created in 1941 by psychologist William Moulton Marston, whose earlier laboratory research helped lay the groundwork for which machine still used in police interrogations today?
source_excerpt: systolic blood pressure test, one component of the modern polygraph

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a superhero creator is a cartoonist or pulp writer; discovering he was a Harvard-trained psychologist whose research fed into the lie detector reframes Wonder Woman's truth-compelling lasso as an inside joke from the inventor himself.
extra.verification_notes: Marston developed the systolic blood pressure test, a component of the modern polygraph, and Wonder Woman debuted in 1941, so 'helped lay the groundwork' is accurate.

explanation: Marston's test measuring changes in blood pressure while someone answered questions is considered a forerunner of the modern lie detector, which makes perfect sense for a heroine whose golden lasso forces anyone caught in it to tell the truth.
